Find the area $A$ bounded by the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $r(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\theta +\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta )){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6} \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6}))+\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}+0 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi })) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }) \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =3(\pi -\frac{\pi }{2})+4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))+\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}-4+\frac{1}{2}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi -8}{2}.\end{aligned}

questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi })) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(\pi -0)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)+\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}+0+\frac{1}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = \cos(3\theta)$ and the lines $\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/350a721c254dab3a8acb2ae54ca5be0bcde6ab036e6936939194c57ae55fe4ff.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = \cos(3\theta),$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{6},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{6},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\theta {|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}((\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6}))+\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{3}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = 1+2\cos\theta$ for $\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{4\pi}{3},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/6bfa0990b560bcb09f2a9eb0b9542296f2a8f1c196b6740702e81c59941d66c5.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = 1+2\cos(\theta),$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},$ this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+2\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -4\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -3\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/d7b39805131dc562e233d49a84f69d30e80ca29cb9443012032d18fdb4512054.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{4},$ as shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta,$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{3\pi}{4},$ this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(4+8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}) \\  & =2\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =2(\frac{3\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{2})-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-1 \\  & =\frac{\pi -2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to find the area of the region bounded by the polar curve $r = 3\cos\theta$ and the rays $\theta_1 = 0$ and $\theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2},$ as shown in blue in the picture below. Can we calculate this area using polar coordinates?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/2c7e638a338aed2155ef5bf388be1f83a3a67d2296d5be09987b099a07edacbd.png)

In general, the area of the region bounded by a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ and the rays $\theta=\theta_1$ and $\theta=\theta_2$ is given by the formula

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2 \:\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Therefore, the area of the half-circle above can be obtained as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){|}_{0}^{\pi /2}) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Intuition Behind the Formula
tutorials.problem:
We've been using the following formula for the area of the region bounded by a polar curve ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/7031a0f3ab71df36bc36e925fcf4f04dbfc4feec5f374092855ef8d97b104452.svg) and the rays ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/38b971de9610efe2ed0de9f10956c73cf5cd967a86a5bcbb076791f369c22bef.svg) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/818e2605a585628c4becd20664b58007dbd2348ca664c80be6a838868a64693a.svg)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/55ffcf934c3a9e33a3376fa1796e6fb68ad1198d719db5ea094fe8eb46c5f47d.svg)

But where does this formula come from?

To see where the formula comes from, we can think about breaking up the area bounded by a polar curve into infinitesimally small sectors of circles.

As shown in the graph below, each sector has a radius of ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/3a4ef1c1b261a53f9c45d0c90f2d44b155125fe1e7b1359406830111b4846f2f.svg) and spans an infinitesimally small angle, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/0904a69fa5e6a3a10eaf74b3fdd865db92761eeeffffae1c0badd33ffdf5b34b.svg)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/82be86e7092a97ca5b2f1423f32b15030af0c8c63bf47ece8be40b45720ac905.png)

The ratio of the area of a sector to the full area of the circle must be the same as the ratio of the angle of the sector to a full revolution of the circle. So, if the area of a sector is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/0b2376d17b173024d6f6c82faaff585293e9830ba7ce0764ecf8338adcd14994.svg) then we can set up and solve the following proportion:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/5d318385ab16ee14d784b33c00180a44ade7cee2e97ffeafd290171d0d44868f.svg)

Finally, to find the area under the curve, we can integrate the areas of all the sectors:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/a75940f74a02ceadff519af028783a0e704fba8a73c4abf36c6a371deb56dee7.svg)
